headline.main: Artificial Intelligence and Deepfakes: The Growing Problem of Fake Porn Images
headline.social: Artificial Intelligence and Deepfakes: The Growing Problem of Fake Porn Images

intro: Thousands of women have been victimized by fake porn images created by artificial intelligence. The victims include minors, celebrities and politicians. DER SPIEGEL went searching for those behind the malicious platforms.
text:
From one day to the next, her daughter had changed completely. Still in grade school, she suddenly became withdrawn and seemed disgusted by her mother. She no longer wanted to cuddle. "We were worried that something might have happened to her that she didn’t want to talk about,” says the mother.
Several months passed before she and her husband found out that their daughter had seen a hardcore porno apparently involving her mother. "She stumbled across the video simply by entering my name into Google,” says Anita Hübig. A well-known German actress, her name has been changed for this story. She has been in the public eye for many years, but she has never taken part in a porn film. "The video was just a few minutes long, but it plunged our family into a deep crisis for many months.”
Their daughter, say Hübig and her husband, was convinced that the film was real and that it showed her mother at a younger age. But it wasn’t. Produced by artificial intelligence, it was a so-called deepfake in which a software program was used to superimpose the mother’s face onto a different body.
Several thousand celebrities have been victimized by such fake sex films in the last seven years – from U.S. mega-star Taylor Swift to leading German politicians. Some of the videos have been watched hundreds of thousands of times, and the platforms that host them rake in millions of clicks per year.
Hübig has insisted on the use of an alias because she is concerned that if she was to discuss the problem using her real name, the videos would receive even more attention.
"It is an awful feeling that somebody edited me into such a film against my will,” she says. Her daughter had to go through therapy, she says, but is now doing much better. "But we’ll never get back the carefree time that we lost. And all because of a short video clip and a Google search.”
In recent years, artificial intelligence has spawned a new, digital form of sexualized violence against women. Images manipulated with Photoshop have been around since the early 2000s, but today, pretty much everybody can produce convincing fakes with just a couple of mouse clicks. And access to these programs is virtually unrestricted.
Unscrupulous entrepreneurs have released a number of programs that can turn a harmless image into a nude photo in just seconds. Or, for a few extra euros, the person concerned can be posed in different sexual positions.
All that is necessary is a snapshot of the victim or a link to their Instagram profile. The anonymous users then receive a high-resolution image that often cannot be distinguished from a real picture. Whether the subject of the photo has given their permission is of no consequence.
Deepfakes also appear in other contexts. During the U.S. presidential campaign, for example, Donald Trump posted AI-generated images with which he wanted to prove that fans of Taylor Swift supported him and not his Democratic adversary, Kamala Harris. But such attempts at political manipulation make up just a tiny fraction of all deepfakes. Surveys have found that more than 90 percent of deepfake videos on the internet are of a sexual nature.
Ninety-nine percent of the victims of such videos are women. Indeed, many of the AI programs that produce naked images can’t even process pictures of men. One app long advertised itself with the slogan: "Imagine wasting time taking her out on dates when you can just use” the website "to get her nudes.”
The operators of such platforms frequently go to great lengths to hide their identities. Many use shell companies or offer their services via the messenger app Telegram. Over the course of many months of reporting, DER SPIEGEL was able to identify several people behind the networks of deepfake services. For the investigation, reporters analyzed data from leaked databases and the source codes of dozens of websites.
Over time, a comprehensive network of deepfake apps from Eastern Europe and Russia emerged. The analyses reveal for the first time just how vast the problem of deepfake videos on the internet has become – and that there is an urgent need for action.
The victims with whom DER SPIEGEL has spoken frequently found themselves having to deal with the digital abuse completely on their own. The number of perpetrators who use such apps is in the many, many thousands.
The Perpetrators
Initially, it was just a niche. In 2017, an anonymous user – screen name "deepfakes” – began rendering celebrities like Scarlett Johansson in explicit sex scenes and posting the results on Reddit. "Doing gods work friend,” wrote one appreciative user about the videos, the quality of which was surprisingly good given the technology available at the time.
When the forum grew to around 90,000 users, Reddit banned it. That was in 2018, but by then, the scene had already become so large that it quickly established its own platform called MrDeepFakes, which remains the largest website for AI-generated sex videos of celebrities. The site’s logo is a grinning cartoon face of Donald Trump holding a mask that is reminiscent of the symbol of the hacker movement Anonymous. The platform went online just three days after the Reddit forum was banned.
These days, it receives more than 6 million visits per month and a DER SPIEGEL analysis found that it includes more than 55,000 fake intimate videos. Tens of thousands of additional videos are uploaded temporarily before being deleted again. In total, the clips have been viewed several billion times in the last seven years.
And the fakes aren’t just a few seconds long. On average, the videos go on for around five-and-a-half minutes.
Were you to play every video continuously one after the other, you could watch fake porno films for 210 straight days.
Producers of the videos can earn money from them, with users able to make special requests for what they want to see for a price, which is paid in Bitcoin. In the last seven years, 300 of the most active users have received more than 2,000 deposits in their crypto wallets. A DER SPIEGEL analysis found that the total volume of Bitcoin transfers is well over 100,000 euros.
Hatred for women and misogyny is everywhere on MrDeepFakes. Left-wing activists portrayed in faked videos on the platform are referred to as "little whores.” A comment beneath a deepfake of a well-known female television presenter in Germany reads: "So this is how the old skank got her own talk show.” Female politicians are frequent targets of such videos, with several women from the top political echelon having been victimized by deepfakes.
In the case of one German minister, DER SPIEGEL has learned, the victim organization HateAid has filed a criminal complaint against the operators of the MrDeepFakes platform. The accusation: Defamation of persons in political life and violation of personality rights through visual imagery.
The police launched a search for the platform’s servers, with investigators saying they happened across IP addresses in California and Mexico City along with servers in the Seychelle Islands. It proved impossible to identify the people responsible for the digital trail, however, and investigators suspect that the operators employ software to cover their digital tracks. The investigation was suspended after nine months. A recent search found 13 faked videos of the minister still online.
The operators apparently believe they are safe. "MrDeepFakes is here to stay,” wrote one of the administrators a few months after the site was launched. "I promise to keep this community running as long as I can.” His username is "dpfks” and he is among the most active and most important administrators of the site. But he and most of the others behind the site have managed to maintain their anonymity.
DER SPIEGEL reporting has found that one of those behind the site is David D., a 36-year-old who lives near the Canadian city of Toronto, where he has been working for several years in a hospital. Among several other indicators, DER SPIEGEL was able to identify him with the help of an email address that was temporarily used as a contact address on the MrDeepFakes platform. He apparently used the same email address privately for a running app. In the last 15 years, D. has registered an astonishing number of websites, many of them apparently rather dubious, as our reporting has found – including a platform for pirating music and software. David D. did not respond to numerous queries about his role with MrDeepFakes.
The Victims
In September 2023, it became clear in the Spanish town of Almendralejo that anybody can be victimized by deepfakes. Graphic, AI-generated images of more than 20 girls in town began circulating on WhatsApp that month. The victims were between 11 and 17 years old.
One of them was the 14-year-old daughter of Mariam Al Adib, a gynecologist. A boy had taken an image from her daughter’s WhatsApp profile and used it to make a fake, she says. "If I didn't know what my daughter looked like naked, I would have thought the pictures were real.”
Shortly after her daughter showed her the AI-generated image, Al Adib uploaded her own video to her Instagram channel, which she normally used to educate her followers on issues related to gynecology. Her video unleashed a wave of indignation about deepfakes in Spain. "It is awful. I feel helpless,” Al Adib says in the video and addresses those responsible for generating the images: "Boys, stop it. Stop producing the images and if you receive one, don’t share it onward. This is no small matter, it’s a criminal offense.”
Al Adib says that her daughter randomly crossed paths out on the street with one of the boys who had made the fakes. He was together with his friends. They started laughing, says Al Adib, and asked her daughter: "Should we take more photos of you."
Al Adib says she was shocked, and furious. "As a doctor, I know that victims of cyber-bullying and sexualized violence sometimes suffer for the rest of their lives.” Some of the girls of whom AI fakes were circulating no longer dared to leave their homes. Others were blackmailed on Instagram with the photos and told to hand over money.
Al Adib ended her 10-minute video with a call to the mothers of other victims to get in touch. Together, they formed a WhatsApp group and filed a complaint with the police.
Some of the officers told the parents that the boys just wanted to have a bit of fun, Al Adib says. "The police only took the case seriously when there was a public outcry in the media.” A juvenile court has since handed the offenders suspended sentences.
Al Adib has become part of a working group under the guidance of the Spanish Ministry of Youth and Children that is looking into the dangers posed to minors by the internet. "As a society, we are completely unaware of the terrible ways in which girls and women can be victimized with the help of AI,” Al Adib says. "We live at a time when it’s not the children who start looking for pornography on the web, rather the pornography comes to them at some point, whether they want it or not.”
Behind the Apps
The nude pictures of Miriam Al Adib’s daughter and the other girls were produced using the service Clothoff. The website remains openly accessible on the web and was visited around 27 million times in the first half of this year. According to an app spokesman, 200,000 images are generated with the help of the app each and every day.
To use the app, all you have to do is confirm that you are over the age of 18 and are only interested in generating naked images of yourself. There are no checks.
The market for such nudify apps is growing. Users are lured in with free pictures, with particularly explicit poses requiring a subscription of between 10 and 50 euros.
But the apps also present a danger to the users themselves. Russian hackers are thought to have launched at least seven such nudify sites with the aim of stealing users’ data. The information is then likely used for other criminal activities, such as credit card fraud.
In San Francisco, meanwhile, a lawsuit is underway against the operators of a number of nudify apps. In some instances, the complaint identifies the defendants by name, but in the case of Clothoff, the accused is only listed as "Doe,” the name frequently used in the U.S. for unknown defendants.
According to the website’s imprint, Clothoff is operated out of the Argentinian capital Buenos Aires. But the company has concealed the true identities of its operators through the use of shell companies and other methods. For a time, operators even sought to mislead  the public with a fake image , presumably generated by AI, of the purported head of Clothoff.
In summer 2024, however, the operators made a misstep: DER SPIEGEL reporting has found that they left an open database online that provided clues as to who is behind the site. While there is no information regarding the alleged head of the company, information from the database in combination with other digital traces allow for the identification of four central figures: the Russian Alexander G., the Belarusians Dasha and Alexander B., who don’t just have the same last name but also the same tattoo, and the Ukrainian Yevgeniy B. The latter stands out in particular: His company was listed in the Clothoff imprint, and in online posts, the 30-year-old claims to value honesty and family. He listed his jobs as web designer and artist, with hobbies that include music and e-sports.
Like the other three, Yevgeniy B. is part of a network of companies from the Russian gaming world, operating sites like CSCase.com, a platform where gamers can purchase additional assets such as special weapons for the game Counterstrike. B.’s company was also listed in the imprint of the site GGsel, a marketplace that includes an offer to Russian gamers for getting around sanctions that prevent them from using the popular U.S. gaming platform Steam. The Belarusian-Russian-Ukrainian network includes at least 10 additional deepfake services and numerous other gaming sites.
None of the four men responded to DER SPIEGEL queries. A person named Elias, identifying himself as a spokesperson for the app, claimed not to know the four. He also said that questions pertaining to the Clothoff team and their specific duties at the company could not be answered due to a "nondisclosure agreement" at the company. Clothoff strictly prohibits the use of photos of people without their consent, he wrote. He also claimed that his service had no connection with the "terrible story” in Almendralejo, insisting that the website’s technology does not process photos of minors. The spokesman declined to provide his last name and telephone number, and he also rejected offers for a video call.
"This isn’t about business," the spokesperson wrote. "We are creating a product for people, for society, with the goal of bringing the fantasies of millions to life without harming others."
Legal Loophole
Silvia Semenzin of Italy once fought successfully to pass a law in her home country that penalizes the publishing of intimate nude images. "Hardly anyone is dealing with these topics because they want to,” says the author and activist. "Almost all of us had bad experiences online.”
In her case, her ex-partner posted intimate videos of her in a WhatsApp group, in which men shared intimate videos of women they slept with. The name of the group: "All Women Are Whores.” Semenzin used it as the title of her book about digital violence against women. She is now fighting for a ban on the production of deepfake nude images without consent. "Almost no member state of the European Union has a sufficient law to protect women against digital violence," she says.
Semenzin is disappointed with how little policymakers have done to protect women from assault both offline and online. "This really shows with the AI Act in the EU." The European Union celebrated the law passed in May as the first far-reaching AI law in the world. The law’s 144 pages regulate many of the risks that could crop up in the future, such as AI-based cyber-attacks and biological weapons or the use of the technology for a military offensive. Nowhere, though, does the AI Act mention the digital abuse of women that is already taking place, nor are there tougher penalties for those who produce deepfakes.
In Germany, state protections are thin. There are no specific legal regulations, and experts say that the production of intimate images of an adult victim using artificial intelligence may not even violate a single regulation in the criminal code. They say that prosecution may be possible on the basis of data protection laws, but such a legal construct has apparently not yet been tested in case law.
Still, when it comes to the dissemination of abusive sexual images, investigators have a slightly easier path. They can use defamation laws or a 1907 statute that protects rights to one’s own image. Germany’s laws, though, are clearly not keeping up with technological developments. Police can usually only take action if victims are prepared to file a criminal complaint – and even still, they have no legal basis to go after those who actually produce the images.
Users of nudify apps, perpetrators in their own right, don’t have much to fear. Payments are frequently anonymous, using Bitcoin, for example. Furthermore, Clothoff operators promise users in the first sentences of the imprint: "We do not save any data.”
That appears to be untrue. DER SPIEGEL was provided a list that includes the identities of thousands of users, including numerous German men. DER SPIEGEL contacted many of them. None responded.
